newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU still has doubts on Boeing/MD merger.
newsitem.headline: EU still has doubts on Boeing/MD merger.

text.p: The European Commission still has serious doubts about the merger of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. despite U.S. Federal Trade Commission clearance for the deal, an European Union source said Wednesday.
"The decision by the FTC in no way changes the serious doubts of the European Commission," the source said.

The Commission, which is expected to rule on the merger by the end of the month, has expressed concern about several aspects of the alliance, including Boeing's exclusive supply deals with three airlines.
The FTC announced in Washington Tuesday that it decided to clear without conditions the $14 billion acquisition by Seattle-based Boeing of McDonnell Douglas, which is based in St. Louis.

FTC commissioners voted four to one not to challenge any aspect of the deal, saying McDonnell Douglas was no longer a competitive force in the commercial aircraft market, an argument the EU executive disputes, the source said.

"Even if the MDC was no longer a viable competitor on a stand-alone basis, its 'competitive potential' taken over by Boeing would considerably strengthen Boeing's already existing dominant position in the market for large commercial aircraft," the source said.

European Commission figures put McDonnell Douglas's share of the global in-service aircraft fleet at 24 percent, a fact the source said would give Boeing access to its former rival's service contracts and spare parts market.

EU anti-trust officials have already made clear their concerns about Boeing's deals on exclusive aircraft supply to several airlines, which they fear would increase as its market share grew from 64 percent to 70 percent after the deals.

The third area worrying the Commission is the danger of spillover into Boeing's commercial aircraft businesses, already the world's largest, from its newly-acquired assets in the defence and space industries.

This point concerns in particular Boeing's greater access to technology developed by publicly-funded research and development in defence and space work, and the company's increased bargaining power with suppliers, the source said.
